opus-5.5.text:
I think the Vision Transformer paper matters less because of any single trick and more because of what it showed about the whole field.

Before ViT, computer vision was dominated by convolutional networks. People believed you needed strong inductive biases like locality and translation equivariance built into the architecture to do well on images. ViT basically said: take an image, cut it into patches, treat each patch like a word token, and feed the sequence into a standard Transformer, almost unchanged from NLP. With enough data and compute, it matched or beat the best CNNs.

That result had a few big consequences.

First, it unified architectures across modalities. Once vision and language could share the same backbone, it became much more natural to build multimodal models. A lot of what we see today, models that take in images, text, and other inputs together, rests on that foundation.

Second, it reinforced the scaling lesson. ViT didn't win on small datasets; it won when you pre-trained at large scale. That told people that hand-designed priors help in low-data regimes, but at scale, a more general architecture can learn those structures from data. That idea shaped how many groups thought about investing in data and compute.

Third, it changed research culture in vision. After ViT, there was a flood of work: hierarchical variants, better training recipes, self-supervised methods like masked image modeling. It opened a new design space, and people moved into it quickly.

From a more theoretical angle, which is something I care about, it also raised interesting questions. Why does attention, with so little built-in structure, end up learning things that look like locality anyway? How do the learned representations emerge during training? Understanding those dynamics is still an open and very interesting problem.

So for me, its influence comes from the simplicity of the idea combined with how far-reaching the implications turned out to be.

r001.rationale: The response says ViT applied a standard Transformer to images, but does not clearly state that it introduced Transformers to computer vision for the first time.

r002.rationale: It says that with enough data and compute, ViT matched or beat the best CNNs, clearly communicating strong vision performance given sufficient data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the Vision Transformer paper matters less for any single trick it introduced and more for what it proved: that the inductive biases we had spent a decade building into convolutional networks were not actually necessary. Before ViT, the whole field assumed that locality, translation equivariance, hierarchical feature maps, all of that, were the reason vision worked. ViT took the plain Transformer from NLP, chopped an image into sixteen-by-sixteen patches, treated them as tokens, and showed that with enough data the model learns those structures on its own. That was a genuine surprise.

The second reason is unification. Once vision and language share the same architecture, you get a single scaling story, a single set of optimization recipes, and a natural path toward multimodal models. A lot of what we now take for granted, from CLIP-style contrastive pretraining to vision-language models, became much simpler to build because both sides spoke the same architectural language.

And the third reason, which I think is underappreciated, is the lesson about data versus architecture. ViT underperformed ResNets on ImageNet alone and only pulled ahead with JFT-scale pretraining. That told the community very clearly that the bottleneck was shifting from clever model design to data and compute. In many ways it was the vision community's version of the scaling-law moment, and it changed how people allocated their research effort afterward.

r001.rationale: The response describes applying a plain Transformer to images, but does not say Vision Transformer introduced Transformers to computer vision for the first time.

r002.rationale: It says ViT showed that, with enough data, the model could learn vision structures and perform well, and notes it pulled ahead of ResNets with JFT-scale pretraining.

astra-6.text:
I think its influence comes from showing that the Transformer isn’t just a model for language. You can take an image, divide it into patches, treat those patches as a sequence of tokens, and apply essentially the same architecture.

Before that, convolutional networks were the standard approach to computer vision. They build in assumptions about images—for example, that nearby pixels are closely related. Vision Transformer raised an interesting question: how much of that structure do we need to build into the model, and how much can it learn from data?

The important qualification is scale. It wasn’t simply that Transformers were better under every condition. With enough data and training, this relatively general architecture could become very competitive. That shifted attention toward how models behave as you scale them.

It also gave vision and language a more common architectural foundation. That makes it easier to bring the two together. So its influence goes beyond image classification; it changed how people thought about building models across different kinds of data.

r001.rationale: The response says Vision Transformer showed that Transformers could be applied to images, but does not claim it introduced them to computer vision for the first time.

r002.rationale: It says that with enough data and training, the architecture could become very competitive, conveying strong vision performance given sufficient data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the Vision Transformer paper was influential because it challenged a very basic assumption in computer vision: that you needed a lot of image-specific structure, like convolutions, to build a strong vision model. It showed that you could divide an image into patches, treat those patches as a sequence of tokens, and apply a Transformer—the same general architecture used in language processing.

There is an important qualification: those image-specific biases are useful, especially when you have limited data. But with enough data and pretraining, a Transformer could learn the relevant relationships and achieve very strong results. That shifted the question from “How do we design a better architecture for images?” toward “How far can we go with a general architecture and more data and computation?”

It also brought vision and language closer together. When both images and text can be represented as tokens and processed with similar architectures, it becomes much easier to think about models that work across modalities. So its influence goes beyond image classification; it helped establish a common foundation for a much broader range of models.

r001.rationale: The response describes applying Transformers to images, but does not say the paper introduced them to computer vision for the first time.

r002.rationale: It says that with enough data and pretraining, a Transformer could achieve very strong results.
